question: How does the radius of curvature of the ice-water interface change with the degree of supercooling during interactions with Tenebrio molitor antifreeze protein?
answer: The radius of curvature of the ice-water interface decreases with increasing supercooling when interacting with Tenebrio molitor antifreeze protein (TmAFP). Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that below the melting temperature, TmAFP allows initial ice growth to form a convex interface, with the radius of curvature being larger at lower supercooling (higher temperatures) and smaller at higher supercooling (lower temperatures). This behavior aligns with the Kelvin effect, demonstrating that greater supercooling leads to a sharper curvature of the ice-water interface, inhibiting further ice growth.

The paper investigates the role of the Kelvin effect in the mechanism of antifreeze proteins (AFPs) using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. The purpose is to provide molecular-level insights into how AFPs inhibit ice growth and melting by altering the curvature of the ice-water interface, thus validating the theoretical predictions of the Kelvin effect.
